DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93, Module 1.

Terminal objective

1.0 Without references, DESCRIBE the components and theory of operation for a diesel engine. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.vi

Enabling objectives

1.1 DEFINE the following diesel engine terms: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.vi

  • a. Compression ratio
  • b. Bore
  • c. Stroke
  • d. Combustion chamber

1.2 Given a drawing of a diesel engine, IDENTIFY the following: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.vi

  • a. Piston/rod
  • b. Cylinder
  • c. Blower
  • d. Crankshaft
  • e. Intake ports or valve(s)
  • f. Exhaust ports or valve(s)
  • g. Fuel injector

1.3 EXPLAIN how a diesel engine converts the chemical energy stored in the diesel fuel into mechanical energy. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.vi

1.4 EXPLAIN how the ignition process occurs in a diesel engine. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.vi

1.5 EXPLAIN the operation of a 4-cycle diesel engine to include when the following events occur during a cycle: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.vi

  • a. Intake
  • b. Exhaust
  • c. Fuel injection
  • d. Compression
  • e. Power

1.6 EXPLAIN the operation of a 2-cycle diesel engine, including when the following events occur during a cycle: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.vii

  • a. Intake
  • b. Exhaust
  • c. Fuel injection
  • d. Compression
  • e. Power

1.7 DESCRIBE how the mechanical-hydraulic governor on a diesel engine controls engine speed. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.vii

1.8 LIST five protective alarms usually found on mid-sized and larger diesel engines. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.vii

What a diesel engine is

Objectives 1.0

"Although several types of prime movers are available (gasoline engines, steam and gas turbines), the diesel engine is the most commonly used." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.1

Diesel engines supply mechanical power for pumping, electrical power generation, operation of heavy equipment, and backup electrical generation during a loss of the normal power source. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.1

A diesel and a gasoline engine are both internal combustion, reciprocating engines. A diesel is heavier than a gasoline engine of equal horsepower because stronger materials must withstand its higher combustion pressures. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.2

"Diesel engines are not self-speed-limiting because the air (oxygen) entering the engine is always the maximum amount." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.3

Engine speed is limited solely by the amount of fuel injected, so a manual fuel control is not possible. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.3

"Diesel engines require a speed limiter, commonly called the governor, to control the amount of fuel being injected into the engine." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.3

Knowledge check: What a diesel engine is

Objective 1.0Q1366

Why is a diesel engine not self-speed-limiting?

The answer is A. Diesel engines are not self-speed-limiting because the air (oxygen) entering the engine is always the maximum amount. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.3

Report a problem
Objective 1.0Q1367

Why is a diesel heavier than a gasoline engine of equal horsepower?

The answer is A. A diesel is heavier due to stronger, heavier materials used to withstand the greater dynamic forces from the higher combustion pressures. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.2

Diesel engine terms

Objectives 1.1

"As previously stated, bore refers to the diameter of the engine's cylinder, and stroke refers to the distance the piston travels from the top of the cylinder to the bottom." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.17
"The highest point of travel by the piston is called top dead center (TDC), and the lowest point of travel is called bottom dead center (BDC)." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.17

The volume enclosed by the sleeve or bore is the combustion chamber, the space where the fuel is burned. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.7

"Displacement refers to the total volume displaced by all the pistons during one stroke." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.17
"Clearance volume is the volume remaining in the cylinder when the piston is at TDC." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.18
"The compression ratio is a measure of how much the engine compresses the gasses in the engine's cylinder." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.3

Compression ratio = (displacement volume + clearance volume) / clearance volume DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.18

"In a diesel engine, compression ratios ranging from 14:1 to as high as 24:1 are commonly used." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.3
"The higher compression ratios are possible because only air is compressed, and then the fuel is injected." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.3

Knowledge check: Diesel engine terms

Objective 1.1Q1368

What is the bore of a diesel engine?

The answer is B. Bore refers to the diameter of the engine's cylinder. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.17

Report a problem
Objective 1.1Q1369

What is the stroke of a diesel engine?

The answer is A. Stroke refers to the distance the piston travels from the top of the cylinder to the bottom. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.17

Report a problem
Objective 1.1Q1370

An engine has a displacement volume of 150 in³ per cylinder and a clearance volume of 10 in³. What is its compression ratio?

The answer is B. Compression ratio = (displacement volume + clearance volume) / clearance volume = (150 + 10) / 10 = 16:1. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.18

Report a problem
Objective 1.1Q1371

Why can a diesel use a higher compression ratio than a gasoline engine?

The answer is A. The higher compression ratios are possible because only air is compressed, and then the fuel is injected. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.3

Major components

Objectives 1.2

The cylinder sleeve or bore confines the combustion gasses and guides the piston. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.6

"The piston transforms the energy of the expanding gasses into mechanical energy." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.7
"These rings function as the seal between the piston and the cylinder wall and also act to reduce friction by minimizing the contact area between the piston and the cylinder wall." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.8
"The connecting rod connects the piston to the crankshaft." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.8
"The crankshaft transforms the linear motion of the pistons into a rotational motion that" DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.8

The rod bearings are offset from the center of the crankshaft, which converts the reciprocating motion of the piston into rotation. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.8

"The amount of offset determines the stroke (distance the piston travels) of the engine (discussed later)." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.8
"Diesel engines have two methods of admitting and exhausting gasses from the cylinder." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.9

Ports are slots in the cylinder walls in the lower third of the bore, opened when the piston travels below them. Valves are in the head casting and are mechanically opened and closed. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.9

"A camshaft is a long bar with egg-shaped eccentric lobes, one lobe for each valve and fuel injector (discussed later)." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.10
"Valve lash is the term given to the "slop" or "give" in the valve train before the cam actually starts to open the valve." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.11
"The diesel engine's blower is part of the air intake system and serves to compress the incoming fresh air for delivery to the cylinders for combustion." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.12

Each cylinder has a fuel injector, which meters and injects fuel at the proper instant. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.30

Objective 1.2Q1372

Which part transforms the linear motion of the pistons into rotation?

The answer is D. The crankshaft transforms the linear motion of the pistons into a rotational motion that is transmitted to the load. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.8

Objective 1.2Q1373

What is the function of the blower?

The answer is A. The blower is part of the air intake system and serves to compress the incoming fresh air for delivery to the cylinders for combustion. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.12

Report a problem
Objective 1.2Q1374

What is valve lash?

The answer is A. Valve lash is the term given to the slop or give in the valve train before the cam actually starts to open the valve. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.11

Report a problem
Objective 1.2Q1375

What do piston rings do?

The answer is D. The rings function as the seal between the piston and the cylinder wall and also act to reduce friction. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.8

Support systems

Objectives 1.0

"A diesel engine requires five supporting systems in order to operate: cooling, lubrication, fuel injection, air intake, and exhaust." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.12

The cooling system is a closed loop with a water pump, radiator or heat exchanger, water jacket, and thermostat. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.12

All moving parts ride on a thin film of oil, pumped from the oil pan through filters into the oil galleries. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.13

"One purpose is to lubricate the bearing surfaces." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.13

The other purpose of the oil is to cool the bearings by absorbing the heat from friction. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.13

"Because diesel engines rely on injectors which are precision components with extremely tight tolerances and very small injection hole(s), the fuel delivered to the engine must be extremely clean and free of contaminants." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.14

Fuel also cools the injectors, so it flows through the engine's fuel system at a rate much higher than needed to run the engine, and the excess is returned. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.14

"The reason for ensuring that an engine's air supply is as cool as possible is that cool air is more dense than hot air." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.15

Per unit volume, cool air has more oxygen, which means a more efficient fuel burn and more power. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.15

"Turbocharging an engine occurs when the engine's own exhaust gasses are forced through a turbine (impeller), which rotates and is connected to a second impeller located in the fresh air intake system." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.16

Compressing the air increases the air forced into each cylinder, which allows more fuel and more power, and the higher intake pressure improves scavenging of exhaust gasses. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.16

Supercharging does the same job with a different power source. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.16

"The blower is driven through gears directly from the engines crankshaft." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.16

The exhaust system routes spent gasses away from the engine, confines and routes them to the turbocharger if used, and allows mufflers to reduce noise. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.16

Knowledge check: Support systems

Objective 1.0Q1376

What five supporting systems does a diesel engine require?

The answer is D. A diesel engine requires five supporting systems: cooling, lubrication, fuel injection, air intake, and exhaust. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.12

Report a problem
Objective 1.0Q1377

Why is diesel fuel kept flowing at a rate much higher than the engine burns?

The answer is A. Fuel serves two purposes: to run the engine and to act as a coolant to the injectors. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.14

Report a problem
Objective 1.0Q1378

What is the difference between turbocharging and supercharging?

The answer is C. Supercharging performs the same function. The difference is the source of power used to drive the device that compresses the air. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.16

Report a problem
Objective 1.0Q1379

Why should engine intake air be as cool as possible?

The answer is A. Cool air is more dense than hot air, so it has more oxygen per unit volume. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.15

From fuel energy to mechanical energy

Objectives 1.3, 1.4

"A diesel engine is a type of heat engine that uses the internal combustion process to convert the energy stored in the chemical bonds of the fuel into useful mechanical energy." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.21
"First, the fuel reacts chemically (burns) and releases energy in the form of heat. Second the heat causes the gasses trapped in the cylinder to expand, and the expanding gases, being confined by the cylinder, must move the piston to expand." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.21
"The reciprocating motion of the piston is then converted into rotational motion by the crankshaft." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.21
"Ignition occurs in a diesel by injecting fuel into the air charge which has been heated by compression to a temperature greater than the ignition point of the fuel." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.28

A diesel needs no ignition system. Fuel is injected as the piston comes to the top of its compression stroke. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.3

"When fuel is injected, it vaporizes and ignites due to the heat created by the compression of the air in the cylinder." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.3

Objective 1.3Q1380

How does the heat of combustion produce mechanical energy in a diesel?

The answer is C. The heat causes the gasses trapped in the cylinder to expand, moving the piston, and the reciprocating motion is converted into rotation by the crankshaft. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.21

Report a problem
Objective 1.4Q1381

What ignites the fuel in a diesel engine?

The answer is B. Ignition occurs by injecting fuel into the air charge which has been heated by compression to a temperature greater than the ignition point of the fuel. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.28

The four-stroke cycle

Objectives 1.5

"To convert the chemical energy of the fuel into useful mechanical energy all internal combustion engines must go through four events: intake, compression, power, and exhaust." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.22
"the engine requires four strokes of the piston (intake, compression, power, and exhaust) to complete one full cycle." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.22

That takes two rotations of the crankshaft, or 720° of crankshaft rotation. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.22

"In a four-stroke engine the camshaft is geared so that it rotates at half the speed of the crankshaft (1:2)." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.22

The timing below is the handbook's generic example for a normally aspirated engine. It varies from engine to engine. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.22

  • Intake: the intake valve starts to open near 28° BTDC while the exhaust valve is still open, and the exhaust valve is fully closed at 23° ATDC
  • Compression: the intake valve is fully closed at 43° ABDC, and the piston compresses the air charge
  • Fuel injection: from 28° BTDC to 3° ATDC
  • Power: after the piston passes TDC, the rise in pressure forces it downward
  • Exhaust: the exhaust valve starts to lift at 48° BBDC, and at 28° BTDC the intake valve opens and the cycle starts again

DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.25

"The time frame during which both the intake and exhaust valves are open is called valve overlap (51° of overlap in this example) and is necessary to allow the fresh air to help scavenge (remove) the spent exhaust gasses and cool the cylinder." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.23
"The fuel enters the cylinder where the heated compressed air is present; however, it will only burn when it is in a vaporized state (attained through the addition of heat to cause vaporization) and intimately mixed with a supply of oxygen." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.24

Knowledge check: The four-stroke cycle

Objective 1.5Q1382

How many crankshaft rotations does one four-stroke cycle take?

The answer is C. A four-stroke engine requires two rotations of the crankshaft, or 720°, to complete one cycle. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.22

Report a problem
Objective 1.5Q1383

At what speed does the camshaft of a four-stroke engine rotate?

The answer is A. In a four-stroke engine the camshaft is geared so that it rotates at half the speed of the crankshaft (1:2). DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.22

Report a problem
Objective 1.5Q1384

What is valve overlap, and why is it needed?

The answer is A. Valve overlap is the time both valves are open, needed to allow the fresh air to help scavenge the spent exhaust gasses and cool the cylinder. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.23

Report a problem
Objective 1.5Q1385

When will injected diesel fuel burn?

The answer is A. Fuel will only burn when it is in a vaporized state and intimately mixed with a supply of oxygen. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.24

The two-stroke cycle

Objectives 1.6

"But a two-stroke engine requires only two strokes of the piston to complete one full cycle." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.25

That takes one rotation of the crankshaft, so several events must occur during each stroke. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.25

"In a two-stroke engine the camshaft is geared so that it rotates at the same speed as the crankshaft (1:1)." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.25

The timing below is the handbook's generic example for a supercharged engine with intake ports and exhaust valves. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.25

  • Exhaust: the exhaust valve lifts off its seat at 91° ATDC
  • Intake: the piston uncovers the inlet ports at 132° ATDC, and compressed fresh air cools and scavenges the cylinder
  • Ports and valve close: the piston closes the intake ports past 48° ABDC, and the exhaust valve is closed at 53° ABDC
  • Compression: temperature and pressure rise after the exhaust valve is on its seat
  • Fuel injection: from 23° BTDC to 6° BTDC
  • Power: from TDC until 91° ATDC, when the exhaust valves start to open and a new cycle begins

DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.27

Engine control and fuel injectors

Objectives 1.0

"The camshaft provides the timing needed to properly inject the fuel, the fuel injector provides the component that meters and injects the fuel, and the governor regulates the amount of fuel that the injector is to inject." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.30

Injectors are actuated by the engine's camshaft, which provides the timing and pumping action. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.30

"The amount of fuel to be injected by each injector is set by a mechanical linkage called the fuel rack." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.30

Rotating the plunger with the fuel rack changes the position of its helices, which changes the amount of fuel injected from no injection to full injection. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.32

The constant flow of fresh, cool fuel through the injector also helps cool it and removes traces of air. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.32

The mechanical-hydraulic governor

Objectives 1.7

"Diesel engine speed is controlled solely by the amount of fuel injected into the engine by the injectors." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.34
"A governor is essentially a speed-sensitive device, designed to maintain a constant engine speed regardless of load variation." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.34
"The position of the flyweights is determined by the speed of the engine." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.35

As the engine speeds up or down, the weights move in or out. That moves a small piston, the pilot valve, in the governor's hydraulic system, which adjusts hydraulic fluid to a large piston, the servo-motor piston. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.35

"The large hydraulic piston is linked to the fuel rack and its motion resets the fuel rack for increased/decreased fuel." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.35
"The reduction in engine speed will be sensed by the governor flyweights." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.37

When load increases, the engine slows and the flyweights move inward. The pilot valve lowers, oil raises the servo-motor piston, and the fuel racks move to increase fuel. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.37

The governor gets its oil from the engine lubricating system. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.34

"This means that a loss of lube oil pressure will cut off the supply of oil to the governor and cause the governor to shut down the engine." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.34

Knowledge check: The mechanical-hydraulic governor

Objective 1.7Q71

A mechanical-hydraulic governor controls diesel engine speed by balancing:

The answer is A. The handbook says the governor balances flyweight engine speed against hydraulic pressure; the other pairs mix parameters from its list of protective alarms and its description of the fuel rack, which the governor positions rather than balances against. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93, Diesel Engine Speed, Fuel Controls, and Protection, ME-01 p. 40

Report a problem
Objective 1.7Q1390

What happens in the governor when engine load increases?

The answer is B. The reduction in speed is sensed by the flyweights, the pilot valve lowers, and the servo-motor piston rises, increasing the fuel injected. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.37

Report a problem
Objective 1.7Q1391

What does a loss of lube oil pressure do to an engine with this type of governor?

The answer is A. A loss of lube oil pressure will cut off the supply of oil to the governor and cause the governor to shut down the engine. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.34

Protective alarms and trips

Objectives 1.8

Protection systems alert operators to abnormal conditions and prevent the engine from destroying itself. Most mid-sized to large engines have at least the five below. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.38

  • Engine overspeed alarm and trip
  • High water jacket temperature alarm
  • High exhaust temperature alarm
  • Low lube oil pressure alarm, trip, or both
  • High crankcase pressure alarm

DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.40

"An overspeed condition is extremely dangerous because engine failure is usually catastrophic and can possibly cause the engine to fly apart." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.38

An overspeed device, usually a mechanical flyweight, cuts off fuel and alarms at a preset rpm. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.39

"The water jacket temperature sensors provide early warning of abnormal engine temperature, usually an alarm function only." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.39
"High exhaust temperature can indicate an overloading of the engine or possible poor performance due to inadequate scavenging (the cooling effect) in the engine." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.39
"Loss of oil pressure can result in the engine seizing due to lack of lubrication." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.39
"Therefore, most medium to larger engines will stop upon low or loss of oil pressure." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.39
"The high pressure condition indicates the engine is in poor condition." DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.40

Worked examples

Objective 1.1

Compression ratio

A cylinder has a displacement volume of 120 in³ and a clearance volume of 8 in³. Find the compression ratio.

  1. Compression ratio = (displacement volume + clearance volume) / clearance volume.
  2. (120 + 8) / 8 = 128 / 8 = 16.

Answer: 16:1, within the 14:1 to 24:1 range the handbook gives for diesels.

DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.18

Objective 1.1

Engine displacement

A six-cylinder engine has a piston area of 9.616 in² and a 4 inch stroke. Find the engine displacement.

  1. Volume of one cylinder = piston area x stroke = 9.616 x 4 = 38.5 in³.
  2. Multiply by the number of cylinders: 38.5 x 6 = 231 in³.

Answer: About 231 in³.

DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.17

Objective 1.5

Force on the piston

Near the top of compression in the handbook's ideal example, cylinder pressure is 742 psia and the piston area is 9.616 in². Find the force on the piston.

  1. Force = pressure x area.
  2. 742 x 9.616 = 7135 lb.

Answer: About 7135 lb, or 3-1/2 tons of force.

DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.23

Objective 1.5

How fast the events happen

A four-stroke diesel runs at a constant 2100 rpm. How long does one stroke take?

  1. 2100 rpm / 60 = 35 revolutions per second.
  2. 35 x 360° = 12,600 degrees per second.
  3. One stroke is 180°, so 180 / 12,600 = 0.01429 seconds.

Answer: About 0.01429 seconds.

DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.22

Summary

  • The diesel is the most common prime mover. It compresses only air, then injects fuel, which ignites from the heat of compression. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.3
  • Bore is cylinder diameter, stroke is piston travel, and the combustion chamber is where the fuel is burned. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.20
  • A four-stroke engine takes two crankshaft rotations per cycle, and a two-stroke engine takes one. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.28
  • A mechanical-hydraulic governor balances flyweights against hydraulic pressure and moves the fuel rack. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.40
  • Usual protection covers overspeed, water jacket temperature, exhaust temperature, lube oil pressure, and crankcase pressure. DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93 ME-01 p.40
